newsitem.title: CANADA: WIC may sell stake in CellularVision.
newsitem.headline: WIC may sell stake in CellularVision.

text.p: Canadian broadcaster WIC's CellularVision wireless subsidiary will seek hundreds of millions of dollars in financing for its new LMCS communications service and may consider sale of a minority stake, CellularVision's president said on Thursday.
"We'll be looking at both equity and debt...We don't anticipate any problem in financing," CellularVision Canada Ltd president Bill Dunbar said in an interview.
CellularVision aimed to be in full service by the third quarter of 1997, Dunbar said.
No financing options were ruled out, Dunbar said.
"We could decide to go for a public offering, an IPO. We could go and find somebody who would want to invest substantial equity into the company," he said.
But WIC Western International Communications Ltd would be unlikely to sell control of CellularVision.
"I can't really speak for the WIC board, but my understanding...is that WIC wants certainly to maintain the majority share of this company for the foreseeable future," Dunbar said.

CellularVision on Tuesday won one of three licenses awarded by the Canadian government for LMCS or local multipoint communications systems. The news sent WIC stock soaring Wednesday and it gained a further 0.50 to 21.75 today.
The other winners were MaxLink and Regional Vision.

MaxLink was 12 percent-held at the time of application by Texas Instruments Inc and by private investors. Regional Vision is 49 percent-owned by Canadian Satellite Communications Inc and 29 percent by a joint venture of SNC-Lavalin Group Inc and Bracknell Corp.

One investment analyst who declined to be identified estimated the service would require investment of C$300 million to C$400 million. Because WIC has a high debt to equity ratio already, "it will need (equity) partners who can provide cash," he said.
Dunbar said CellularVision initially intended to be a carrier for service providers such as long-distance telephone companies or Internet access companies.
"To start with, our intention is to be basically a services carrier, mainly providing services to other people," he said.

But that could change if it got requests to offer services directly. It eventually may also deliver signals for broadcasters, which could open up cross-fertilization opportunities with WIC's broadcasting operations, he said.
WIC owns eight television stations including a stake in Canada's CTV network and 12 radio stations.
WIC began research into LMCS in 1992, acquired the Canadian rights to an analog version of the technology in 1993 and said it was the first company to develop a digital version.
